heroText: Porto-Novo is Benin's low-key political capital, a lagoon-side city of Afro-Brazilian architecture and Yoruba heritage overshadowed in size by nearby Cotonou. First-time visitors should tour the Musée Honmè inside the old royal palace, browse the stalls at Ouando Market, and admire the Grand Mosque of Porto-Novo, built in Afro-Brazilian style by returned freed slaves. Cardinal Bernardin Gantin International Airport in Cotonou is the nearest gateway, about an hour's drive away.

areas.name: Colonial District (Centre-ville)
areas.text: The Colonial District centres on 19th- and 20th-century Afro-Brazilian buildings around the royal palace, the best base for walking to museums and the cathedral.

areas.name: Ouando
areas.text: Ouando sits about 3 kilometres north of the centre around Benin's largest market, a livelier district with more nightlife than the historic core.

areas.name: Akron
areas.text: Akron is one of Porto-Novo's oldest neighbourhoods, tracing back to early settlement and useful for a quieter, more local stay near the lagoon.

airports.name: Cardinal Bernardin Gantin International Airport (COO)
airports.search: Cardinal Bernardin Gantin International Airport, Cotonou, Benin
airports.text: Cardinal Bernardin Gantin International Airport is in Cotonou, roughly 40 kilometres and about an hour's drive from Porto-Novo; arrange a taxi or transfer in advance.

airportTransfer.value: Compare road transfer time between Cardinal Bernardin Gantin International Airport (COO) and central Porto-Novo before choosing an airport-area or city-centre hotel.

stayOverview: Stay in the Colonial District for walking access to the royal palace, museums and cathedral, or choose Ouando for a livelier base near the main market. Most travellers fly into Cotonou and treat Porto-Novo as an easy day trip or one-night stop.
hotelIntro: Accommodation in Porto-Novo is more limited and modest than in Cotonou, so the Colonial District suits travellers prioritizing sightseeing on foot, while Ouando offers simpler guesthouses closer to the market and everyday local life.
rentalCars: A rental car is not needed inside compact Porto-Novo, but one or a hired driver helps for the day trip to Cotonou or Ganvié.

travelTips.title: Best base
travelTips.text: Stay in the Colonial District for easy walks to the royal palace, museums and cathedral, or Ouando if you want to be near the main market.

travelTips.title: Airport access
travelTips.text: Fly into Cotonou's Cardinal Bernardin Gantin International Airport and budget about an hour for the road transfer to Porto-Novo.

travelTips.title: Language and cash
travelTips.text: French is the official language and cash is preferred for markets and small vendors, so carry West African CFA francs in small denominations.

travelTips.title: Day trips
travelTips.text: Combine Porto-Novo with a half-day visit to Ganvié's stilt villages or an evening in Cotonou, both reachable within a couple of hours.

nearbyIdeas.text: Cotonou is Benin's largest city and economic capital, an easy day trip from Porto-Novo for shopping, dining and the international airport.

history.text: In 1861, the British, who were active in nearby Nigeria, bombarded the city, which caused the Kingdom of Porto-Novo to accept the French offer of protection in 1863.
In 1883, Porto-Novo was incorporated into the French "colony of Dahomey and its dependencies" and in 1900, it became Dahomey's capital city.
From 1908, the king held the title of Chef supérieur.
The kings of Porto-Novo continued to rule in the city, both officially and unofficially, until the death of the last king, Alohinto Gbeffa, in 1976.

history.label: Growth
history.text: It remains untranslated in French, the national language of Benin.

history.label: Modern city
history.text: Porto-Novo was once a tributary of the Yoruba Oyo Empire, which had offered it protection from the neighbouring Fon, who were expanding their influence and power in the region.

history.label: Today
history.text: Today, the Yoruba community in Porto-Novo remains one of the two original ethnic groups in the city.

history.label: Civic role
history.text: The city was originally called Ajashe (Àjàṣẹ́ in Yoruba orthography) by the Yorubas, and Hogbonu by the Gun.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: The neighbouring Kingdom of Dahomey objected to French involvement in the region and war broke out between the two states.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: Unlike the city's earlier Gun migrants, however, the French sought to impose their language in all spheres of life and completely stamp out the use and proliferation of indigenous languages.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: Many Afro-Brazilians settled in Porto-Novo following their return to Africa after emancipation in Brazil.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: Brazilian architecture and foods are important to the city's cultural life.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: Under French colonial rule, flight across the new border to British-ruled Nigeria in order to avoid harsh taxation, military service and forced labour was common.
